title: Waypoint
teaser: A retirement tracker with an agentic coach to simplify one question: "Am I on track for retirement?"

sections.problem: I wanted to explore how I could take an amortization calculator that many might use for retirement analysis, model more financial scenarios, implement far more Monte Carlo scenarios, and result in a justifiable number for whether a user is on or off track for retirement. Adding an agentic coach was there to serve as supplementary to a financial advisor and was aimed to especially think about what if scenarios that play out through the models, as in for every dollar put in a certain financial vehicle today, what it looks like at your desired retirement age along with how inflation impacts your purchasing power at that point.
sections.build: A retirement tracker built around a series of snapshots. It starts with who the person is and what they'd like to have at retirement, then each check-in logs their accounts and projects whether they're ahead, on track, or worth a closer look against the age and number they said they want. The projection comes from 250 seeded simulated paths rather than a single guess, and because it's saved at each check-in, Waypoint can later compare what it predicted against what actually happened. An optional Coach writes a short assessment with one or two suggestions, aimed at pointing the user in a direction rather than handing down a verdict.
sections.technical: An HTML/JS front end running on a small Node.js/Express server, with settings and check-ins persisted to local JSON files and the projection engine kept in its own module. The Coach is an agentic call to the Claude Code CLI on the user's own machine, and it sends the user's profile, balances, projection, notes, and recent analyses to Anthropic under their own account; everything else stays local. The public demo is a self-contained static build running the same projection math on a fictional persona, with one real Coach analysis generated on that persona's data and saved into the file.
sections.learning: The biggest challenge was simplification: letting a user bring difficult financial scenarios while the modeling stays behind the scenes. There is no right answer, per se, when running a whole host of Monte Carlo scenarios to arrive at a justifiable, defensible number, so keeping the build atomic enough to allow for sensible aggregation was the hardest part. Learning was also really working with the right balance of finding the agentic voice. Fine tuning the coach from not hallucinating too much but also not handing a user completely obvious information was the balance being sought. Where I eventually aimed the output was more akin to pointing a user in a certain direction and using the math to drive the "if then" portion of the justification of the recommendation.
sections.next: I'd like to continue to find more financial vehicles to model into the scenario along with adding a coach tone selection. I started with a balanced coach, but some users would likely prefer even softer treatment whereas other users would want more brass tacks from the coach to kick them into shape if they were off track.
